Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Situation2: They set aside part of their routine to light a lamp and offer prayers at their home altar.
Story: It was almost 9 p.m. when my phone buzzed with a call from Riya. Her voice trembled as she told me her car had broken down on the highway, miles from home, and she was scared. She needed me to come get her right away. My heart raced—I knew how anxious she got in the dark, and as her friend, I felt a deep responsibility to help her, no matter the hour. But as I glanced at the clock, I realized it was nearly time for my evening puja. Every night, I light a lamp and offer prayers at my home altar, a ritual that grounds me and honors my faith. Missing it feels wrong, almost like breaking a promise to myself and to the divine. The expectation to be there for my friend clashed with my commitment to my spiritual practice. I stood in the hallway, keys in one hand and the matchbox in the other, torn between rushing out the door and staying to complete my prayers, my mind swirling with guilt and worry from both sides.
